45 min

Mendelian randomization in Diversity Outbred mice with qtl2mr

CTC 2026 workshop · 45 minutes

Two traits move together. Which one drives the other? We answer that with genetics, in R, on simulated Diversity Outbred (DO) mice where we know the right answer.

Xiaoyang Dai · University of Bristol

How to follow

  • Light boxes are R code. Copy each one into the RStudio Console, in order, in the same R session.
  • Dark boxes show the Console output you should see.
  • Figures appear in the Plots pane and are saved in results/.
  • More detail boxes are for later; the talk does not need them.

Before class: set up at home

Install and test at home: in class there is no time to fix installations.

  1. Install R 4.1 or newer from CRAN and RStudio Desktop from posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop.
  2. Get the workshop folder from github.com/XDai-bris/qtl2mr-tutorial: click Code → Download ZIP and unzip it, or run git clone https://github.com/XDai-bris/qtl2mr-tutorial.Windows: keep the folder outside OneDrive or Dropbox; synced folders often block package installation.
  3. In RStudio, choose File → Open Project… and open qtl2mr-tutorial.Rproj in that folder.
  4. Copy the Task 01 box below into the RStudio Console and press Enter. It installs qtl2mr 0.6.0 from the folder into a private library/ folder inside the project, so nothing else on your computer changes. It needs the internet once, to download the small fs package.Linux: fs is built from source and needs libuv (libuv1-dev on Debian and Ubuntu).

More detailWhat Task 01 does, and where the code lives

R/install.R checks that the bundled file package/qtl2mr_0.6.0.tar.gz is the unchanged qtl2mr 0.6.0 release, installs it into the project's library/ folder and checks the version. R/setup.R loads the small helpers in R/ (tables, figures, and the two-sample and SNP helpers used in Tasks 04 and 05) and starts a new folder results/run_…, where every figure is saved. Every qtl2mr call that selects instruments or fits a model is visible in the task code.

Each light box in this guide is one part of a file in tasks/; workshop.R holds all five tasks in one script. The last decimal place of some numbers may differ between computers.

Tested on macOS with R 4.6.2. GitHub also replays all five tasks automatically on Windows, macOS and Linux, and with R 4.1, and compares the Console output with this guide; the badge in the README shows the latest result.

Opening · 4 min · 00–04

Two traits move together. Which drives which?

An association is not a cause. Genetics can help us tell the two apart.

In your mice, animals with more X tend to have more Y. Three stories fit that pattern: X raises Y; Y raises X; or a third factor, U, raises both. An association mixes all three: cause, shared causes and reverse direction. We call the possible cause, X, the exposure, and the trait it may change, Y, the outcome.

Mendelian randomization (MR) uses the random inheritance of alleles to isolate the causal part. Which allele a mouse inherits is decided at random when its parents pass on their chromosomes, and it is fixed at conception, so neither X nor Y can change it. If a genetic variant G changes X, the mice that inherited the X-raising allele received, in effect, a small randomly assigned dose of X. If those mice also differ in Y, the difference travelled through X, provided three assumptions hold.

  1. 1G affects X: the variant really changes the exposure.
  2. 2G is independent of U: the hidden factors that move both traits do not decide which allele a mouse inherits.
  3. 3G affects Y only through X: there is no other path from the variant to the outcome.
More detailWords used in this guide
Exposure and outcome
X, the possible cause, is the exposure; Y, the trait it may change, is the outcome.
Instrument
A genetic variant used like G in the diagram. In DO mice our instruments are QTL for the exposure.
Founders
DO mice descend from eight inbred founder strains, labelled A to H. At each locus, each chromosome copy comes from one founder.
LOD score
The evidence from a QTL scan that a marker is associated with a trait; higher means stronger.
F (founder F, F_X_block)
How strongly the eight founder alleles at one locus, taken together, predict the exposure: the joint Wald statistic of the seven founder contrasts, divided by 7. Larger means stronger; it does not show that an instrument is valid.
Kinship
How related two mice are. qtl2mr uses it to allow for relatedness, as qtl2 does in QTL scans.
95% interval
The range of values compatible with the data under the model. The intervals in this guide are nominal: they assume the model is right, and their coverage was not checked in this example.

0.5 · Meet the simulated world · 3 min · 04–07

Meet the simulated world

We built this world, so we know the right answer and can check every method against it.

  • X → Y: effect 0.5. One unit more X causes half a unit more Y.
  • U raises both X and Y. U is hidden: it is not in the data.
  • Y has no effect on X.
  • QTL for Y act on Y directly; Part 1 uses them for the reverse question.

Genotypes were simulated with simcross (Karl Broman; CRAN), and traits with qtl2founderSim. From one DO-like population we drew three cohorts of 400 mice that share no mouse:

Cohort 1400 mice · X and Y measuredPart 1
Cohort A400 mice · X onlyPart 2
Cohort B400 mice · Y onlyPart 2

You do not generate any data: Task 02 loads it from data/.

R · Task 02 · tasks/02_world.R
cat("\nTASK 02 | Meet the simulated world\n")
# Three groups of 400 mice from one simulated Diversity Outbred population.
cohort1 <- readRDS("data/cohort1.rds")  # X and Y measured
cohortA <- readRDS("data/cohortA.rds")  # only X measured
cohortB <- readRDS("data/cohortB.rds")  # only Y measured
show_table(data.frame(cohort = c("Cohort 1", "Cohort A", "Cohort B"),
                      mice = c(nrow(cohort1$pheno), nrow(cohortA$pheno), nrow(cohortB$pheno)),
                      measured = c("X and Y", "X only", "Y only")))
cat("Each cohort file holds:", paste(names(cohort1), collapse = ", "), "\n")
# The truth built into the simulation:
# X raises Y by 0.5; Y has no effect on X; a hidden factor U raises both.
show_table(data.frame(mouse = rownames(cohort1$pheno)[1:5], head(cohort1$pheno, 5)))
cat("Markers:", nrow(cohort1$map), "on", length(unique(cohort1$map$chr)), "chromosomes\n")
show_table(head(cohort1$map, 3))
plot_founder_bars(cohort1, marker = "chr2_050")
plot_kinship(cohort1)
cat("Milestone 2: founder probabilities, kinship, traits and scans are loaded.\n")

One row per mouse, with X and Y in simulated units, and 1500 markers on 19 chromosomes. Each cohort file holds what qtl2 users already have: founder probabilities (genoprobs), kinship, phenotypes, the marker map and the QTL scans.

More detailHow this world was built

X is controlled by 10 QTL, each with its own founder pattern: five split the founders into two groups, like a SNP, and five have three or more levels. Y has 4 QTL of its own, on other chromosomes. A hidden factor U raises both X and Y, X raises Y by 0.5, and the QTL for X affect Y only through X. The population was simulated with simcross's DO breeding design (20 generations of outbreeding from the eight founders).

The scans in data/ were computed in advance with qtl2 (scan1(), with leave-one-chromosome-out kinship). Simplifications: founder probabilities are exact (in real data they are estimated from SNP genotypes and are less clean), with no genotyping error, no covariates and no X chromosome.

All settings were fixed in advance. A simulated world was accepted only if pre-set design checks passed (enough copies of every founder allele, strong enough QTL for X and for Y, an association of the expected size); no MR result was used to choose it, and nothing was tuned afterwards.

Part 1 · 14 min · 07–21

Correlation is not causation

In Cohort 1 the association between X and Y is about twice the causal effect; MR recovers the effect and its direction.

1AThe association

Fit a straight line of Y against X (a regression) in the 400 mice of Cohort 1. The slope says how much Y changes, on average, with one unit more X.

R · Task 03A · tasks/03_correlation_vs_causation.R
# PART A | Correlation: the observational slope
cat("\nTASK 03A | Cohort 1: how much does Y change with X?\n")
obs <- lm(Y ~ X, data = cohort1$pheno)
obs_ci <- confint(obs)["X", ]
show_table(data.frame(slope = coef(obs)[["X"]], lower = obs_ci[[1]], upper = obs_ci[[2]]))
cat("The true causal effect is 0.5. The hidden U also moves X and Y together.\n")
Console output · reference run
TASK 03A | Cohort 1: how much does Y change with X?
 slope lower upper
 0.962 0.747 1.176
The true causal effect is 0.5. The hidden U also moves X and Y together.

The slope is 0.962, with a 95% interval (the range of values compatible with the data) of 0.747 to 1.176: about 1, twice the true effect of 0.5. The extra half comes from U, which pushes X and Y up together. More mice would only make the interval narrower, around the wrong number.

1BMR from X to Y

Choose instruments. Instruments are QTL for X. The scan for X was run in advance with qtl2. We keep the top marker of each region with LOD ≥ 3, and only if its founder F is at least 4. F measures how strongly the eight founder alleles at that locus, together, predict X.

Estimate. At each instrument, qtl2mr estimates the eight founder effects on X and on Y, then finds the one slope that best links the Y pattern to the X pattern across all instruments. That slope is the MR estimate.

R · Task 03B · tasks/03_correlation_vs_causation.R
# PART B | MR from X to Y
cat("\nTASK 03B | MR from X to Y in Cohort 1\n")
resources1 <- qtl2mr_prepare_resources(
  allele_probs = cohort1$genoprobs, kinship = cohort1$kinship,
  pheno = cohort1$pheno, covar = NULL, marker_map = cohort1$map
)
# Instruments: one peak per region with LOD >= 3, kept if its founder F >= 4.
instruments_x <- qtl2mr_select_instruments(
  resources1, cohort1$scan[, "X", drop = FALSE], exposures = "X",
  lod_thresh = 3, F_X_min = 4, progress = FALSE
)
show_table(instruments_x[instruments_x$selected, c("marker", "chr", "pos", "lod", "F_X_block")])
mr_xy <- run_qtl2mr_analysis(
  qtl2mr_pair_input(resources1, instruments_x, exposure = "X", outcome = "Y"),
  output_dir = file.path(run_dir, "mr_x_to_y"), standardize_phenotypes = FALSE,
  heterogeneity_method = "chisq", diagnostic_bootstrap_B = 0L,
  run_loo_mr = FALSE, run_instrument_sensitivity = FALSE,
  make_html = FALSE, make_figures = FALSE, verbose = FALSE, progress = FALSE
)
show_table(summary(mr_xy)[, c("exposure", "outcome", "n_loci", "estimate", "ci_lower", "ci_upper")])

This block takes about 10 seconds. Wait for the > prompt before the next one.

11 instruments pass the rules. The MR estimate is 0.48 (95% interval 0.255 to 0.693). It contains the truth, 0.5, and excludes the association, 0.962.

More detailThe idea behind the MR slope

Take one instrument. Suppose inheriting founder C instead of an average founder raises X by 1 unit and Y by 0.5 units. If the instrument changes Y only through X, one unit of X causes 0.5 units of Y. qtl2mr uses all eight founder effects at each instrument, combines the instruments, and allows for the uncertainty of both the X and the Y effects.

More detailThe settings in the code

standardize_phenotypes = FALSE keeps X and Y in their own units, so the estimate can be compared with the truth, 0.5. The bootstrap, leave-one-out and instrument-sensitivity analyses are switched off to keep the run short; see the qtl2mr documentation before using these settings on your own data. The MR intervals are nominal 95% profile intervals.

More detailOne instrument is a chance finding

Because we built the world, we know where the true QTL are. One of the 11 instruments, chr15_006, has no true X-QTL nearby: it passed both rules by chance. The rules were fixed in advance and are not adjusted after seeing the results, so it stays. Instruments chosen and used in the same mice can carry chance associations like this; that is one reason for the two-sample design in Part 2.

1CMR from Y to X, and the three answers

Now the reverse question: does Y affect X? Instruments for Y must change Y and must not act on X directly. QTL for X also move Y a little, through X, so a Y peak could sit on an X-QTL. As a simple rule, we drop any Y peak whose X LOD at the same marker is 3 or more.

R · Task 03C · tasks/03_correlation_vs_causation.R
# PART C | MR from Y to X, and the three answers side by side
cat("\nTASK 03C | MR from Y to X in Cohort 1\n")
instruments_y <- qtl2mr_select_instruments(
  resources1, cohort1$scan[, "Y", drop = FALSE], exposures = "Y",
  lod_thresh = 3, F_X_min = 4, progress = FALSE
)
# Use loci linked to Y but not to X: X LOD below 3 at the same marker.
instruments_y$x_lod <- cohort1$scan[instruments_y$marker, "X"]
instruments_y$selected <- instruments_y$selected & instruments_y$x_lod < 3
keep_y <- instruments_y[instruments_y$selected, ]
show_table(data.frame(marker = keep_y$marker, chr = keep_y$chr, lod_Y = keep_y$lod,
                      F_Y = keep_y$F_X_block, lod_X = keep_y$x_lod))
mr_yx <- run_qtl2mr_analysis(
  qtl2mr_pair_input(resources1, instruments_y, exposure = "Y", outcome = "X"),
  output_dir = file.path(run_dir, "mr_y_to_x"), standardize_phenotypes = FALSE,
  heterogeneity_method = "chisq", diagnostic_bootstrap_B = 0L,
  run_loo_mr = FALSE, run_instrument_sensitivity = FALSE,
  make_html = FALSE, make_figures = FALSE, verbose = FALSE, progress = FALSE
)
s_xy <- summary(mr_xy)
s_yx <- summary(mr_yx)
answers <- data.frame(
  question = c("Observational (Y on X)", "MR X -> Y", "MR Y -> X"),
  estimate = c(coef(obs)[["X"]], s_xy$estimate, s_yx$estimate),
  lower = c(obs_ci[[1]], s_xy$ci_lower, s_yx$ci_lower),
  upper = c(obs_ci[[2]], s_xy$ci_upper, s_yx$ci_upper),
  truth = c(NA, 0.5, 0)
)
show_table(answers)
answers$label <- c("Observational\n(Y on X)", paste("MR X", arrow, "Y"), paste("MR Y", arrow, "X"))
plot_summary(answers)
cat("Milestone 3: the association (slope about 1) is not the causal effect (0.5); MR recovers the arrow.\n")

Milestone 3: the association (slope about 1) is not the causal effect (0.5); MR recovers the arrow.

What we see

  • The association, 0.962, is inflated by U.
  • MR X → Y, 0.48, is close to the truth of 0.5.
  • MR Y → X, 0.012 (95% interval −0.053 to 0.069), is close to 0: no sign that Y drives X, so the evidence points from X to Y.

MR gives evidence about cause only under the three assumptions in the diagram; here the simulation was built so that they hold for the true QTL (chance findings aside); with real data they have to be argued.

More detailA chance Y instrument, and what “close to 0” means

One of the 5 Y instruments, chr4_088, has no true QTL either: it passed the fixed rules by chance and stays, as the rules require. An interval around 0 does not prove that there is no effect; it says that any effect of Y on X is likely to be small, here between −0.053 and 0.069 under the model.

If Y did affect X, its true QTL would also show some X signal, so this filter can pull the Y → X estimate toward 0; it is a teaching simplification.

Part 2 · 12 min · 21–33

Two-sample MR

X and Y were never measured in the same mice, so no association can be computed. Yet MR estimates the effect.

Cohort A measured only X; Cohort B measured only Y. No mouse has both, so there is no X–Y association to compute at all. MR needs only two pieces for each instrument: its effect on X, from Cohort A, and the effect of the same locus on Y, from Cohort B. These effects, with their uncertainty (standard errors and covariances), can come from published founder-effect estimates, or be estimated with qtl2mr from founder probabilities and phenotypes on a shared marker map, as here. Two-sample MR assumes both cohorts come from the same population, so each locus has the same effect on X in both.

2AInstruments from Cohort A, read off in Cohort B

R · Task 04A · tasks/04_two_sample.R
# PART A | Instruments from Cohort A, looked up in Cohort B
cat("\nTASK 04A | Find X instruments in Cohort A\n")
resourcesA <- qtl2mr_prepare_resources(
  allele_probs = cohortA$genoprobs, kinship = cohortA$kinship,
  pheno = cohortA$pheno, covar = NULL, marker_map = cohortA$map
)
instruments_a <- qtl2mr_select_instruments(
  resourcesA, cohortA$scan, exposures = "X",
  lod_thresh = 3, F_X_min = 4, progress = FALSE
)
markers <- instruments_a$marker[instruments_a$selected]
show_table(instruments_a[instruments_a$selected, c("marker", "chr", "pos", "lod", "F_X_block")])
cat("Mice with both X and Y:", length(intersect(rownames(cohortA$pheno), rownames(cohortB$pheno))), "\n")
plot_miami(cohortA, cohortB, markers)

Cohort A gives 9 X instruments, and no mouse has both X and Y. Cohort B's Y scan peaks on chromosomes 3, 8, 12 and 18, the QTL of Y itself, and stays low under the instrument lines. The Y scan need not peak there: an X-QTL moves Y only through X, a small push among everything else that moves Y. MR does not look for Y peaks; it asks whether each instrument's founder pattern shows up in Y, scaled by one common factor: the MR slope.

More detailWhy 9 instruments, not 10 or 11?

In Cohort 1 the same rules found an instrument on chromosome 4 (chr4_023). In Cohort A this true X-QTL narrowly missed the F ≥ 4 rule, so the two-sample fit uses 9 instruments. The rules are fixed in advance; we do not lower them after seeing the results. The chance instrument of Cohort 1, chr15_006, did not pass in Cohort A.

2BTwo-sample MR

For each instrument, fit the eight founder effects on X in Cohort A and on Y in Cohort B. The small helper two_sample_block(), in R/mr_helpers.R, puts the two fits together and records that their errors are independent, because no mouse is in both cohorts. fit_multilocus_founder_mr() then finds the common slope.

R · Task 04B · tasks/04_two_sample.R
# PART B | Two-sample MR
cat("\nTASK 04B | X effects from Cohort A, Y effects from Cohort B\n")
x_in_A <- setNames(cohortA$pheno$X, rownames(cohortA$pheno))
y_in_B <- setNames(cohortB$pheno$Y, rownames(cohortB$pheno))
blocks <- lapply(markers, function(m) {
  chr <- cohortA$map$chr[cohortA$map$marker == m]
  fit_x <- fit_founder_lmm_block(cohortA$genoprobs, x_in_A, kinship = cohortA$kinship[[chr]], marker = m)
  fit_y <- fit_founder_lmm_block(cohortB$genoprobs, y_in_B, kinship = cohortB$kinship[[chr]], marker = m)
  two_sample_block(fit_x, fit_y)
})
mr_2s <- fit_multilocus_founder_mr(blocks, allow_cross_cov = FALSE,
                                   compute_independence = FALSE, heterogeneity_method = "chisq")
show_table(data.frame(n_loci = length(blocks), estimate = mr_2s$theta,
                      lower = mr_2s$profile_ci_lower, upper = mr_2s$profile_ci_upper,
                      interval = mr_2s$confidence_set_type))
Console output · reference run
TASK 04B | X effects from Cohort A, Y effects from Cohort B
 n_loci estimate lower upper interval
      9     0.49 0.206 0.784  bounded

Two-sample MR gives 0.49 (95% interval 0.206 to 0.784; bounded means one finite interval). It contains the truth, 0.5. The interval is wider than in Cohort 1, partly because there are 9 instruments instead of 11. Two-sample use of qtl2mr 0.6.0 is not yet formally validated; here the known truth is the check.

More detailTwo-sample MR with qtl2mr 0.6.0

Because X and Y come from different mice, this task uses qtl2mr's lower-level functions, fit_founder_lmm_block() and fit_multilocus_founder_mr(), with the X–Y error covariance set to zero (allow_cross_cov = FALSE). Cohorts A and B come from one population and include relatives; the fit treats them as independent, which is a simplification.

2CThe MR scatter: one point per instrument

R · Task 04C · tasks/04_two_sample.R
# PART C | The MR scatter: one point per instrument
cat("\nTASK 04C | Plot the instruments\n")
points_2s <- do.call(rbind, lapply(blocks, locus_point))
show_table(points_2s)
plot_mr_scatter(points_2s, theta = mr_2s$theta)
founders_2s <- do.call(rbind, lapply(blocks, function(b) {
  data.frame(marker = b$marker, founder = rownames(b$fit_x$founder_H),
             x = founder_effects(b$fit_x)$effect, y = founder_effects(b$fit_y)$effect)
}))
plot_founder_scatter(founders_2s, theta = mr_2s$theta)
cat("Milestone 4: no mouse has both traits, yet MR estimates the effect of X on Y.\n")

More detailWhy the MR line looks a little steep for the points

A line drawn by eye, or by simple regression, through these points would be a little flatter than the MR line. The X values are estimates with their own noise, and noise in X flattens a simple regression line (regression dilution). The MR estimator allows for the uncertainty in the X effects and is designed to avoid this flattening. That is why the figure shows the MR line and the truth, not a line fitted through the points.

More detailEvery founder at every instrument

A single founder's effect on Y is estimated with a lot of noise, so the cloud is wide; the MR line (0.49) and the truth (0.5) carry the message. MR uses all eight founder effects at each instrument, taking their uncertainty into account, rather than any single dot.

Part 3 · 5 min · 33–38

Built for DO mice

In DO mice a QTL is an eight-founder pattern, not two alleles, and qtl2mr uses the whole pattern.

DO mice descend from eight founder strains, A to H. At one QTL each founder's haplotype can have its own effect, so a QTL can have up to eight levels. A SNP has only two alleles: it splits the founders into two groups and can miss the rest of the pattern.

R · Task 05A · tasks/05_founders.R
# PART A | One QTL: eight founder effects, or one SNP?
cat("\nTASK 05A | A QTL is an 8-founder pattern\n")
locus <- blocks[[match("chr11_027", markers)]]
founder_x <- founder_effects(locus$fit_x)
show_table(founder_x)
snp <- best_snp(locus$fit_x)
cat("Best single SNP: founders", paste(snp, collapse = ""), "against the rest\n")
plot_founder_vs_snp(founder_x, snp, snp_effect(locus$fit_x, snp), locus$marker)
Console output · reference run
TASK 05A | A QTL is an 8-founder pattern
 founder effect    se
       A -0.123 0.262
       B  0.107 0.194
       C  0.752 0.156
       D   0.03 0.152
       E -0.053 0.161
       F  0.011  0.21
       G -0.601 0.162
       H -0.123 0.239
Best single SNP: founders C against the rest
Figure saved: figures/07_founders_vs_snp.png

At chr11_027, founder C raises X (0.752) and founder G lowers it (−0.601); the other six founders are close to 0. The best single SNP, C against the rest, captures C but lumps G in with the other six. qtl2mr keeps all eight effects.

You already have the inputs. qtl2mr starts from the objects qtl2 users already have:

Founder probabilitiesqtl2 genoprobs, as allele probabilities, go into qtl2mr_prepare_resources().
Kinshipqtl2 calc_kinship() output, one matrix per chromosome (leave one chromosome out), also goes into qtl2mr_prepare_resources().
QTL scanqtl2 scan1() LOD scores go into qtl2mr_select_instruments().
More detailHow the best SNP is chosen

There are 127 ways to split eight founders into carriers and non-carriers. best_snp(), in R/mr_helpers.R, picks the split most strongly associated with X: the lead SNP that a SNP-based study would find. snp_effect() reads the eight-founder fit along that split. In the simulation, the true pattern at this QTL is exactly what the founder effects show: one founder up (C) and another down (G).

In qtl2, allele probabilities come from genoprob_to_alleleprob() and leave-one-chromosome-out kinship from calc_kinship(type = "loco").

Take-home · 4 min · 38–42

Take-home

Three points, one for each part.

  1. An association is not a causal effect: here it was about twice the truth (0.962 against 0.5), while MR recovered the effect (0.48) and its direction, as evidence that holds under the three assumptions.
  2. Two-sample MR estimated the effect (0.49) from X measured in one cohort and Y in another, where no association could be computed at all.
  3. qtl2mr is built for DO mice: it reads each QTL as an eight-founder pattern, not two alleles, and starts from the founder probabilities, kinship and scans that qtl2 users already have.

To use qtl2mr on your own data, install the latest release from github.com/XDai-bris/qtl2mr-uvmr. Questions are welcome on GitHub issues or by email to x.dai@bristol.ac.uk.

3.5 · Extension, if time allows · 3 min · 42–45

Founder-based vs SNP-based MR

On these data the founder-based interval is only slightly narrower than the SNP-based one: a modest gain.

Same mice and the same 9 instruments; the only change is that each instrument is reduced to its best single SNP, as a SNP-based study would do.

R · Task 05B · tasks/05_founders.R
# PART B | Extension: founder-based vs SNP-based MR on the same mice
cat("\nTASK 05B | Founder-based vs SNP-based two-sample MR\n")
snp_table <- do.call(rbind, lapply(blocks, function(b) {
  s <- best_snp(b$fit_x)  # picked with X in Cohort A, as a SNP study would
  ex <- snp_effect(b$fit_x, s)
  ey <- snp_effect(b$fit_y, s)
  founder_signal <- drop(t(b$beta_x) %*% solve(b$Sigma_x) %*% b$beta_x)
  data.frame(marker = b$marker, chr = b$chr, snp = paste(s, collapse = ""),
             bx = ex[["effect"]], se_x = ex[["se"]], by = ey[["effect"]], se_y = ey[["se"]],
             share = (ex[["effect"]] / ex[["se"]])^2 / founder_signal)
}))
show_table(snp_table[, c("marker", "snp", "share")])
mr_snp <- second_order_gls_ivw(snp_table$bx, snp_table$by,
                               diag(snp_table$se_x^2), diag(snp_table$se_y^2))
comparison <- data.frame(
  method = c("Founder", "SNP"),
  estimate = c(mr_2s$theta, mr_snp$theta),
  lower = c(mr_2s$profile_ci_lower, mr_snp$profile_ci_lower),
  upper = c(mr_2s$profile_ci_upper, mr_snp$profile_ci_upper)
)
comparison$width <- comparison$upper - comparison$lower
show_table(comparison)
plot_founder_vs_snp_precision(comparison, snp_table)
cat("Milestone 5: founder effects keep the whole pattern; a SNP keeps one split.\n")

Figure saved: figures/08_founder_vs_snp_precision.png 
Milestone 5: founder effects keep the whole pattern; a SNP keeps one split.

Both methods land near the truth (founder 0.49, SNP 0.478). The founder-based interval is 0.577 wide and the SNP-based one 0.601: about 4% narrower. That gain is modest here: at 5 of the 9 instruments the true pattern has just two groups, which one SNP can capture. The bars show the share of the association statistic kept by the best SNP: between 0.665 and 0.92.

More detailWhat the bars measure

Share = the best SNP's association statistic for X (1 degree of freedom) divided by the eight-founder statistic (7 degrees of freedom) at the same locus. The bars stay below 1 even where the true pattern has two groups, because the eight-founder statistic also picks up noise in the directions that carry no signal. So they show the share of the association statistic kept by the SNP, not exactly the information lost. The SNP effects here are read off the eight-founder fit (projected onto the SNP split, with the same variance components) rather than taken from a separate SNP scan, so the comparison is slightly favourable to the SNP side. How much founder-based MR gains depends on how many QTL have patterns with more than two levels; with other data the gain can be larger or smaller.
